author: bradknowles
storyTitle: The multiple meanings of “nameserver” and “DNS resolver”
text:
As someone who has been involved in DNS and BIND in one capacity or another since about 1991 (and a technical reviewer of The O’Reilly book “DNS and BIND” by Cricket Liu and Paul Albitz), I have a much simpler definition in mind.
A nameserver is a piece of software that runs independently in the background (as a “daemon”) on a host or VM, and answers queries from resolvers or other name servers, possibly locally on the machine, or locally to the current private subnet, or publicly, or some combination there of. It might run in caching-only mode, it might run in authoritative mode, or it might (inadvisedly) run in both caching and authoritative mode. Unless running in authoritative-only mode, to be a nameserver means that you must support recursion. If you are not running in authoritative mode, and you do not support recursion, then you are not a nameserver.
A resolver is a bit of library code that other code might call, but does not run independently. Moreover, resolvers are generally less capable than nameservers, and might even be single-threaded. Their only real purpose is to take the simple queries that they get from clients to the library, and to turn those into real DNS queries that can be addressed to a nameserver, usually a caching nameserver because resolvers aren’t generally that bright, and they can’t do their own recursion. But a nameserver can do recursion, if it is not running in authoritative-only mode.
The program “nsd” is an authoritative-only nameserver, see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSD
In contrast, “unbound” is a caching-only recursive nameserver, see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbound_(DNS_server)
Both programs were developed under the auspices of NLNet.
For examples of a DNS resolver, the first obvious stop is whatever version of libc that you have installed, and the gethostby* library calls.
That’s the way I see it.

And it cannot be eliminated at all; I've seen the namuwiki, the biggest Korean encyclopedic wiki [1] besides from Wikipedia, falling into this trap and turning itself into a slew of toxic contents.
I had been long against a single big wiki model like Wikipedia. It unbelievably works, and it seems that it will thrive even with the insurmountable amount of cracks, but we need alternatives (plural)---fully accountable, easy-to-fork and community-free. And we don't yet have a single alternative taking off (for example I really wanted Infinithree/Thunkpedia to thrive [2]). Every time I ponder about this, I come back to the circle and find myself searching for the Shii's great piece [3]. I don't exactly agree to the suggestion to simply make a personal "wiki", for the lack of forking mechanism, but the entire essay is still surpringly true, and possibly the only viable alternative to Wikipedia because it clearly lacks the community. I'm still waiting for others.
